items.q: What qualifies as a small package shipment?
items.a: Any parcel typically under 150 lbs. and within specific size limits, shipped via carriers like UPS, FedEx, or USPS.

items.q: What's the difference between ground and express shipping?
items.a: Ground is more economical with longer delivery times. Express (Next Day, 2nd Day) is faster and costs more.

items.q: How are small package rates calculated?
items.a: Rates depend on package weight, dimensions, delivery speed, distance, and any surcharges.

items.q: What is dimensional (DIM) weight?
items.a: DIM weight is calculated using package size, not just weight. It ensures large, light boxes don't cost too little to ship.

items.q: Can I schedule a pickup for small packages?
items.a: Yes, most carriers offer scheduled or on-demand pickups, often for a small fee.

items.q: Is tracking included with small package shipping?
items.a: Yes, all major carriers offer detailed tracking from pickup to final delivery.

items.q: What happens if a package is lost or delayed?
items.a: You can file a claim. Most carriers offer guaranteed delivery times for express services and basic insurance coverage.

items.q: Do I need special packaging for small parcels?
items.a: Standard corrugated boxes work well. Use protective materials for fragile items, and make sure to label clearly.

items.q: Can I insure my small package?
items.a: Yes, additional insurance is available beyond the default coverage (usually $100 value with most carriers).

items.q: How do I save money on small package shipping?
items.a: Use negotiated carrier rates, ship with zone optimization, and consolidate shipments when possible.

items.q: What is LTL shipping?
items.a: LTL (Less-Than-Truckload) shipping is used when freight doesn't require a full truck. Multiple shipments from different shippers share space and cost on the same truck.

items.q: When should I use LTL shipping?
items.a: LTL is ideal for shipments between 150–15,000 lbs. that don't require an entire trailer. It's cost-effective for smaller freight volumes.

items.q: How are LTL shipping rates calculated?
items.a: Rates are based on freight class, weight, distance, dimensions, and additional services like liftgate or residential delivery.

items.q: What is freight class and why does it matter?
items.a: Freight class (NMFC) is a standardized classification that impacts cost. It's determined by density, handling, stowability, and liability.

items.q: Can I track my LTL shipment?
items.a: Yes, most carriers offer tracking via PRO number or BOL number through their online portals or customer service.

items.q: How long does LTL shipping take?
items.a: Transit times depend on the origin and destination but typically range from 1 to 7 business days.

items.q: What documents are needed for LTL shipping?
items.a: A Bill of Lading (BOL) is the primary document. It serves as a receipt and contract between shipper and carrier.

items.q: Is my freight insured in LTL shipping?
items.a: Basic carrier liability is included but often limited. Additional freight insurance is recommended for higher-value shipments.

items.q: What if my shipment is damaged or lost?
items.a: You can file a freight claim with the carrier. Document the damage with photos, save all packaging and paperwork, and notify the carrier at delivery or as soon as possible.

items.q: Do I need a forklift or dock for LTL delivery?
items.a: Not necessarily. If you don't have a dock or forklift, request a liftgate service at pickup or delivery for an extra fee. Some carriers allow the product to be unloaded by hand to avoid additional liftgate fees.

items.q: What is full truckload (FTL) shipping?
items.a: FTL shipping means your freight exclusively occupies a truck. It's faster and safer for larger shipments.

items.q: When should I use FTL shipping?
items.a: Use FTL for shipments over 15,000 lbs., high-value or fragile items, or when you need faster transit times.

items.q: How is FTL pricing determined?
items.a: Pricing is based on mileage, route, equipment type, fuel cost, and market demand — but not freight class.

items.q: What equipment types are available for FTL?
items.a: Common options include dry vans, flatbeds, and refrigerated (reefer) trailers.

items.q: Is FTL faster than LTL shipping?
items.a: Yes, FTL is typically faster because the truck goes directly from pickup to delivery without handling other freight.

items.q: Can I track my FTL shipment?
items.a: Yes, many carriers provide GPS tracking or location updates from the driver or dispatch.

items.q: What accessorial charges should I expect with FTL?
items.a: Possible charges include detention, layover, truck ordered not used (TONU), and lumper fees.

items.q: Do I need to palletize my freight for FTL?
items.a: Not always. You can ship loose or floor-loaded items if secured properly, though palletizing helps with loading and safety.

items.q: Is insurance included with FTL?
items.a: Yes, but like LTL, it's limited. Consider additional cargo insurance for high-value freight.

items.q: What's the lead time for scheduling an FTL shipment?
items.a: Same-day shipping is possible, but booking 24–48 hours in advance ensures better availability and pricing.
